Data complexity has recently been recognized as a more objective indicator of learning difficulty than the imbalance ratio alone, because class overlap and complex decision boundaries often impair classifiers more severely than imbalance itself. Samples near the decision boundary are inherently difficult to classify, which has motivated many researchers to focus on such instances to improve classifier performance. However, most under-sampling approaches fail to differentiate their sampling of boundary samples across datasets of varying complexity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a complexity-adaptive boundary-aware ensemble (CBE) framework that links the sampling weight distribution to data complexity and dynamically adjusts the boundary preference of under-sampling accordingly. We also introduce an overall complexity measure that combines metrics at multiple levels and use it to divide imbalanced datasets into three categories. Extensive experiments on 24 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL show that the proposed method outperforms many existing methods in terms of F-measure and G-mean on Easy and Median datasets, without degrading performance on hard cases.

title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
author: Fail Gafarov
abstract: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.

title: Achieving Minimax-Optimal First-Order and Best-of-Both-Worlds Regret Simultaneously in Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Mengxiao Zhang
abstract: We study first-order and best-of-both-worlds regret guarantees in multi-armed bandits. Pogodin and Lattimore (2019) proposed an algorithm that combines minimax-optimal worst-case regret with a first-order guarantee whose loss-dependent term is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star}\log T)$, where $T$ denotes the horizon, $L^\star$ denotes the smallest expected cumulative loss among fixed arms, and $K$ denotes the number of arms. However, a logarithmic gap remains between this loss-dependent term and the optimal first-order scale. In this paper, we remove this logarithmic factor by proposing an efficient and parameter-free algorithm that achieves the minimax optimal first-order regret guarantee $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star})$. Technically, our algorithm is built upon FTRL with a Tsallis entropy regularizer (Zimmert and Seldin,2021), with a learning rate adapted to the learner's cumulative loss and a sampling distribution determined by a scalar fixed point. This construction controls the combined estimation and stability cost in terms of the learner's loss. Moreover, we show that the same algorithm achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee, with $\mathcal{O}(\sum_{i\ne i^\star}\frac{\log T}{Δ_i})$ regret for i.i.d. losses with a unique best arm $i^\star$, where $Δ_i$ denotes the suboptimality gap of arm $i$.

title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
author: Fareed Sheriff
abstract: Masked diffusion models train a denoiser on masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel. Existing MDM sampling bounds assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled while training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained. We present an end-to-end guarantee for a learned denoiser under conditional mixing (CM): stationary sources (e.g. floored order-$r$ Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources) for which revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token's posterior on average exponentially little in the distance with correlation length $τ_c$. We show the empirical risk minimizer trained under any masking distribution attains per-token excess $\varepsilon'$ on that distribution from $\varepsilon'^{-\mathcal{O}(τ_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)}$ training sequences, independent of sequence length $N$ -- one sample budget serves every decoding schedule when each schedule's denoiser is trained under its own weighting. We further show that the exponent's order $Θ(τ_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)$ is minimax-optimal up to constants; more efficient rates require added structure. With this, we bound the end-to-end KL as $\mathrm{KL}(π\Vert p_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq \varepsilon+N\varepsilon'$ under a dilated schedule of $T=\mathcal{O}(τ_c\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon))$ denoising steps versus $Ω(N)$ steps for a fixed random order on an explicit CM source. Finally, we show that block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error and that a $Λ$-looped order-$r$ message-passing class on order-$r$ sources achieves polynomial sample complexity, with approximation error improving per loop until saturation at $Λr\approx τ_c\log(1/\varepsilon')$. Experiments on released and retrained models support our results' qualitative predictions.

title: Diameter-two graphs whose mutual-visibility chromatic number equals their chromatic number
author: Siddhesh Chaubal
abstract: A set $S$ of vertices of a graph $G$ is a mutual-visibility set if every pair of vertices of $S$ is joined by a shortest path whose internal vertices avoid $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $χ_μ(G)$ is the least number of mutual-visibility sets into which $V(G)$ can be partitioned. Klavžar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero (2025) proved that $χ_μ(G)\leχ(G)$ whenever $G$ has diameter two, observed that equality holds for complete bipartite graphs, and asked whether there are any other diameter-two graphs attaining equality. We answer this question in the affirmative. We construct a graph $G_{11}$ of order 11 and diameter two with $χ_μ(G_{11})=χ(G_{11})=3$, and an infinite family of such graphs obtained from $G_{11}$ by replacing one vertex with pairwise non-adjacent copies of it.

title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
author: Oleg Vasilyev
abstract: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses, but the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.

title: Information-Driven Collaborative Autonomy for Heterogeneous UAV/UGV Teams
author: Joshua Yuriv Pilipovsky
abstract: This paper considers coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) traversing a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, adapting their trajectories to ground routes and target information. We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization. The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view footprints and pose-dependent probabilistic detection models. Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets. This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization. Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats. We solve each team's optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*--C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints. A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets' trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold. Numerical case studies examine sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs.

title: Limit Theorems and Optimal Policies for Flock Flight through Poisson Forests
author: Lav R. Varshney
abstract: Inspired by birds flying through cluttered environments, Karaman and Frazzoli showed that high-speed flight through an ergodic random forest exhibits an ultimate speed limit: above a critical speed, almost surely no infinite collision-free trajectory exists for a single bird. This paper formulates a corresponding bulk-transport problem for many birds. We construct an explicit directed corridor network in a Poisson disk forest and impose a common temporal headway at its waypoints. The maximum current equals a minimum vertex-cut capacity and is achieved by repeated flight along vertex-disjoint paths. The same schedule maximizes completed traversals at every finite horizon, with constant forward speed and no internal waiting. For a forest belt of fixed depth, exact transverse superadditivity yields an almost-sure deterministic current-density limit. A uniform shape theorem for an asymmetric planar dual identifies the current when depth and width grow together. For diverging depth bounded by a constant times width, this current equals the width-first, depth-second limit and is independent of the positive aspect ratio. When diagonal corridors are available, bulk current is positive at sufficiently low obstacle intensity and zero at sufficiently high intensity. For stochastic demand, an upstream admission queue is stable at every rate below the finite-network capacity.

title: A Uniform Upper Bound on the Length of MDS Codes from Genus-Two Curves
author: Haojie Chen
abstract: We study the maximal length of MDS algebraic geometry codes from genus-two curves over finite fields. Let $C_\mathcal{ L}(D,G)$ be such a code over $\mathbb F_q$, with length $n$ and dimension $k$. Assume that $3\leq k\leq n-3$. We prove that $n<(2q+10\sqrt q+16)/3$. This bound holds for every prime power $q$ and for both parities of $k$. It gives a uniform upper bound of $2q/3+O(\sqrt q)$ for the maximal length. The explicit bound is strictly smaller than $q+1$ when $q\geq125$.

title: Construction and formal verification of a special topology on {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}: characterization of connected subsets
author: Ignacio Vega-Páez
abstract: We examine whether the integers admit a topology whose connected subsets are precisely the sets of consecutive integers. The main result gives a construction for every integer lattice {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, n>0; the answer for Z is then obtained as a corollary. We prove that the neighborhoods determined by the parity of the sum of the coordinates form a basis and that topological connectedness agrees exactly with accessibility by finite paths of unit lattice steps. We also present a deductive audit and the correspondence between this argument and a verification in Lean 4 and Mathlib, including the empty set and the independent formal characterization of integer intervals. The construction and mathematical result originate in Problem 5712, proposed by Dan Marcus and solved in 1970 by the Cleveland State University group; the present article contributes a detailed exposition and a report on formal verification.

title: CoToan: Executable Rules and a Representation Contract for Reproducible Game AI Evaluation
author: Ha-Thanh Nguyen
abstract: Game AI results are comparable only when different implementations expose the same decision problem. Yet seemingly minor representation choices can silently change that problem by altering action probabilities or collapsing states with different outcomes. We study this issue through CoToan, an executable specification and representation contract for Vietnamese Mathematical Chess connecting the Game Description Language (GDL) with OpenSpiel. The game provides a useful case because a single capture may have multiple arithmetic justifications, while outcomes can depend on scoring rules and a finite playing horizon. CoToan therefore represents actions by their state transitions rather than by arithmetic witnesses, and treats time and victory configuration as part of task identity. Cross-representation tests show agreement in legal actions, successor states, and terminal outcomes across hundreds of sampled and constructed positions, complemented by exhaustive checks of all 32 operator masks and 512 opposing-material subsets. Controlled diagnostics further show that uniform witness-level sampling alters endpoint-action probabilities, while omitting remaining time or victory settings can merge states with different terminal behavior. These results show that action semantics, time, and victory configuration are not merely implementation details. They are part of the experimental task itself and must be represented explicitly for reproducible game AI.

title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories
author: Tidor-Vlad Pricope
abstract: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.

title: Telling Is Not Seeing: Textual Personas Rarely Make Vision-Language Models Answer Like the People They Describe
author: Jiawei Chen
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly prompted with personas, such as "You have low vision", to stand in for people in user studies. We ask whether a persona makes a model see like the person it describes. We compare persona answers with measured people with low vision, color blindness or hearing loss, and with simple rules that use only the facts the persona states. The persona never beats these rules, and it erases the real differences between groups and individuals. Describing blur leaves recognition unchanged in all 14 models we test, while blurring the photo lowers it as it does for people. Inside open models, the description changes neither the image information nor the answer probabilities. Yet the models know the effects they fail to show: they can estimate how blur and illusions affect people. Telling is not seeing: a persona makes a model say what it knows about people, not see what they see.

title: There Is No Free Lunch in RLVR: Every pass@1 Gain Has a pass@k Price
author: Yinuo Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes a language model solve more problems on the first try and fewer when given many tries: it raises pass@1 while the base model overtakes it at large sampling budget k. Is this a failure of RL to add reasoning, or a transient that more training removes? We settle the question with a theorem. The reversal is a price, and we compute its exact rate. Modeling RLVR as an exponential tilt of a base policy over strategies shared across prompts, we prove that under exclusive specialization every update that raises pass@1 strictly lowers the success of some prompt; a strictly positive price on prompts (Stiemke duality) is the exact condition, and being merely the best strategy on a prompt is provably not enough. When the loss reaches the hardest prompts, it forces a pass@k crossover, and the number of crossings is at most the sign variation of the shift in per-prompt success, a totally positive bound that is tight and that recovers the known single-crossover result as its order-preserving case. The crossover is not a bug to patch: a constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the entire pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity yields entropy collapse and the entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent, unifying two literatures under one mechanism. Reinforcement cannot widen the reasoning frontier; it can only move along it, at a price we make measurable by a diagnostic that reads the bound, the order-preserving test, and the price from any evaluation log. There is no free lunch, only a price.

title: What Does "Now" Mean to Your Computer-Use Agent? Stale Screenshots, Page Loads, and Which Check to Run Before a Click
author: Vasundra Srinivasan
abstract: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click at a position on the screen; if the page has changed in the meantime, the click lands on an unintended element. Prior work treats the planning interval as the source of this risk. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, we find that the risk lies in page loading: 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. On these pages, waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial pages keep loading for longer: in the HTTP Archive's public crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of their HTML being parsed, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages, and 52% shifted their layout within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds, against 8% (61% against 26% among pages recorded in full). Where a check before the click is needed, as before irreversible actions and on pages that are still loading, a pixel comparison verifies the target's position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, and a 4B model matches the frontier model in verifying whether the previous action succeeded. We release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers: https://github.com/multimodal-ai-engineering/preflight-bench

title: Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification
author: Zhiheng Zhang
abstract: Continuous-integration evidence is conditional: a workflow determines which jobs should run, while an archive records which jobs remain observable. Reconstructing requirements from those observations lets an omission erase its own obligation. We present a qualification method that compiles a pinned workflow into conditional job requirements independently of target presence, retains a fixed capture inventory, and checks source-complete derivation certificates with a separate implementation. For a fixed source, context, scope and binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization. The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes from evidence coverage. Both implementations match the 45 hand-specified authorization controls, reject 180 source-certificate attacks, and exhibit no authorization gain over 704 distinct proper development erasures. An explicitly witnessed 12-job platform run qualifies in both implementations; all 4,095 proper payload-subset erasures block authorization. A frozen collection spans 240 runs in eight workflow families across six projects. All 160 evaluation source certificates independently validate, but unavailable historical execution-source identities leave actual qualification open. Initial gate diagnoses agree on 155/160 runs; a preserved unknown-propagation repair yields 160/160 agreement in a retrospective rerun. The study establishes bounded source extraction and omission resistance, rather than natural-fault prevalence or producer authenticity.

title: XLaw-JP-27B: A Lightweight Open Model Specialized for Japanese Law
author: Andrew Shin
abstract: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at https://x-law.jp/ with the weights available at https://huggingface.co/X-LawJapan/xlaw-jp-27b under Apache~2.0.

title: Mathematics and Efficiency of Song's CVP Hardness Reduction
author: Shuhong Gao
abstract: Song (2026) proves that, for every fixed $0<ε<1$, the closest codeword problem (CCP) for binary linear codes under Hamming distance is NP-hard to approximate within $N^{1-ε}$, where $N$ is the code length, under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The code-to-lattice construction gives hardness within $N^{1/2-ε/2}$ for Euclidean CVP, with the same $N$ aslattice rank. This reaches every fixed Euclidean hardness exponent below one half. Aharonov and Regev (2005), with the constant refined by Gao (2026), place GapCVP at factor $cN^{1/2}$ in $\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}$ for every fixed $c>2/(π\sqrt3)\approx0.3676$. NP-hardness at that scale would imply $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$. This paper has two goals: to explain Song's theorem and its mathematics for graduate students, and to make the reduction more efficient. The reduction turns satisfiability into a system of quadratic equations and then into CCP for binary linear codes, and recovers assignments from recurrence relations of algebraic moments. We adapt the method to linear codes over any fixed finite field of characteristic $p$. A common recurrence for each block column gives a moment window $L=c_p(κ-1)+1$, where $c_p=\max\{2,p-1\}$ and $κ$ is the rank cutoff. Together with ordinary digit products and flexible sampling, this reduces interpolation degrees and output lengths. For CCP gap $N^{1-ε}$, our explicit schedule gives code length and lattice rank at most $n^{4/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$; Song's prescribed binary schedule gives $n^{8/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$. Here $n$ counts variables in a common quadratic system, equal to the number of original variables plus clauses for 3SAT. These are dimension bounds, not optimality claims or running-time exponents. The limiting hardness exponents remain Song's.

title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
author: Cheng Zhang
abstract: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.

title: Zero-Complement Extrapolation: Parameter Recovery and Classification in Severely Imbalanced Logistic Regression under Rank-Deficient Regimes
author: Chongsun Park
abstract: Parameter estimation and classification in binary logistic regression deteriorate severely when the number of minority class observations ($n_1$) is smaller than the feature dimension ($p$). Under such rank-deficient rarity ($n_1 < p$), maximum likelihood estimators suffer from quasi-complete separation, penalized likelihood methods exhibit severe intercept bias, and convex minority oversampling techniques such as SMOTE collapse into an $(n_1 - 1)$-dimensional affine subspace. In this paper, we propose a novel \textit{Self-Calibrated Zero-Complement} estimator that shifts the paradigm from minority interpolation to majority fringe extrapolation. Grounded in Stein's Lemma, we prove that the conditional expectation shift of the abundant majority class ($Y=0$) induced by logistic truncation uniquely identifies the true hyperplane normal $\boldsymbolβ$ after Mahalanobis whitening. We further establish that extrapolating synthetic minority instances outward from the high-quantile density fringe of the majority distribution along the conjugate direction preserves full-rank covariance regularity ($\mathrm{rank} = p$). To accommodate both semi-supervised environments (with an unlabeled background mean) and strictly supervised subsamples, we introduce a hybrid estimator incorporating the intrinsic third-moment skewness of the majority class alongside a location-shift-invariant zero-boundary intercept calibration. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations and real-world benchmark applications (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer and Banknote Authentication) under extreme rarity ($n_1 \in \{3, 5\}$) demonstrate that our approach prevents parameter divergence, recovers the oracle hyperplane with high fidelity, and substantially outperforms Firth's regression and SMOTE in F1-score and estimation stability.

title: Reading-Level Verification of Kanji Words in Japanese Financial Speech Synthesis
author: Cheng Zhang
abstract: Few-shot voice cloning makes it cheap to produce daily Japanese financial commentary with several synthetic speakers, but kanji words with more than one reading, such as the word for "market" (shijo vs. ichiba) or "overall trend" (taisei vs. oze), are still misread. A common quality gate transcribes each synthesized sentence with automatic speech recognition (ASR), converts both the input and the transcript to kana, and regenerates on mismatch. We show that this gate is unreliable in both directions: when the audio contains a misreading, the ASR language model frequently writes the expected kanji back, hiding the error, and when the audio is correct, ordinary recognition errors trigger needless regeneration. We propose a reading-level check that scores the expected reading and its confusable alternatives with a connectionist temporal classification (CTC) hiragana recognizer and flags a word when an alternative explains the audio better. On 540 utterances from three voice-cloned production voices covering 30 financial terms, with misreadings injected under controlled conditions, the transcript-based gate detected 78.9% of misreadings at a 44.4% false-alarm rate, whereas the proposed check detected 91.7% at 5.0% (AUC 0.990). On natural kanji input, it caught a front-end error that the transcript-based gate missed for one voice, and reduced regeneration requests from 38.9% to 6.1% of sentences.

title: Kinematic Causal Attribution: Black-Box Explanations of Motion versus Geometry for 4D Point-Cloud Video Models
author: Zerui Wang
abstract: 4D perception models, which classify 3D point-cloud videos, are being built into robots, assistive monitoring and AR, yet before deploying one a practitioner cannot check which cue it relies on: how a body part moves, or what shape it has. 3D attribution is single-frame, video attribution is confined to RGB pixels, gradient maps need white-box access, attention is absent from state-space backbones, and point-level perturbations assume a point correspondence across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack. We present Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA), a black-box, interventional attribution method that queries only the model's outputs. Its freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes the shape while keeping the motion. Together they span a motion$\times$geometry cube for every tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured rather than assumed away. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so they need no correspondences, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures that span several regions. We validate KCA on the official PSTNet, P4Transformer and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D. The decisive test is an audit: two binary tasks are built from real clips whose classes differ only in the motion or only in the shape of the same arm, and the motion share of the arm's importance follows the defining cue on all three backbones (0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D), a distinction no single attribution map can make. The split costs no faithfulness: the necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet, tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D, and lose their correlation with the trained model's once the weights are randomised. Skeleton ground truth, re-sampling stability and cost complete the validation.

title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers
author: Irfan Tekdir
abstract: In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
author: Bravish Ghosh
abstract: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

title: Building On Learning-Augmented Online Sorting
author: Wyatt Olson
abstract: Online sorting is a problem that has gained attention recently, and is a natural translation of sorting into an online setting. The problem at hand is to place elements of an online sequence immediately and irrevocably with the goal of producing an array that is as close to sorted as possible upon inserting all elements. Recent work by Bercea et al. [ESA 2026] introduced the incorporation of learned predictions into the online sorting domain. They show lower bounds for the consistency and robustness of any algorithm, including randomization, then provide a deterministic algorithm that is $O(n/r)$-consistent and $O(r)$-robust, which are tight bounds. However, this algorithm requires prior knowledge of the optimal offline cost of the full input sequence before all elements have been revealed. We resolve this by providing an algorithm with matching bounds that does not require knowledge of the optimal cost, then extend these results to the more general problem of online metric TSP, in line with the prior work.

title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
author: Prashant Chaudhary
abstract: Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts. Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced. Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison. Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser. Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.

title: Comparing wins above replacement across baseball history
author: Michael Doane
abstract: This paper introduces iWAR, a system for estimating wins above replacement from historical Retrosheet play-by-play records. We compare its runs-allowed (RA) and fielding-independent pitching (FIP) versions with Baseball-Reference WAR (bWAR), FanGraphs WAR (fWAR) and run-based alternatives. The common historical sample contains 1,471 team-seasons across 79 years and 1,441 consecutive franchise pairs. Under the fixed conversion to wins, same-season mean absolute error was 3.695 credited wins per 162 games for iWAR RA, compared with 4.724 for bWAR and 4.744 for fWAR: reductions of 21.793% and 22.112%. The paired differences were -1.030 and -1.049, with conditional 95% calendar-block intervals of [-1.367, -0.706] and [-1.398, -0.725]. Calibration preserved most of these advantages. A broader bWAR comparison across 118 years retained a smaller advantage; modern differences were smaller or sometimes reversed. PythagenPat reconstructed records more closely than every WAR total. Next-season replay gave nearly identical fixed-map errors for iWAR FIP and fWAR, while calibration changed their ordering. An amended chronological learned-model analysis of 1,552 franchise pairs gave neural RMSE 10.163, versus 9.946 for the development-selected ridge comparator (difference +0.217; conditional interval [0.015, 0.474]). This work provides a new, specialized framework for analyzing WAR across eras and provides context for future work using learning models.

title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk
author: Ebrahim Khaled Ebrahim
abstract: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC's within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.

title: How Hard Is It to Compute Cover Time?
author: Ryan Aghazadeh
abstract: It is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$. Even for connected simple undirected unweighted graphs, deciding whether an expected random-walk cover time is at most a given rational threshold is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$ under polynomial-time Turing reductions, both from a specified starting vertex and when maximized over starting vertices. Both families have a universal vertex, called the hub, and diameter two. Deleting the hub leaves a planar bipartite graph, and every non-hub vertex has degree at most five. A shared construction encodes an Euler-tour count in rare covering walks. For specified starts, a number of fractional bits linear in the queried graph's vertex count suffices for recovery. For the maximum-start problem, a fixed cube attachment makes the maximizing starts known, and one interpolation of expected cover times recovers the count. Both reductions use polynomial-size graphs and polynomial-bit threshold queries. For general graphs, both comparison problems can be solved in polynomial time with access to an $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{PP}}$ oracle.

title: Beyond atol and rtol: Sound Test Oracles for Low-Precision GPU Kernels
author: Xinyi Shi
abstract: Low-precision GPU kernels are commonly tested against a reference using hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances. Legitimate numerical error varies with the input, format and precision plan, so a fixed tolerance trades false alarms for missed faults. We present numoracle, which derives per-element acceptance regions from precision-annotated reference programs. Its calculus tracks shared rounding errors, provenance-ordered products, block-scaled quantizers and calibrated math-library errors. A rounding-interval check detects faulty stores that symmetric bounds can admit. Soundness is conditional on explicit rounding, hardware, domain and implementation assumptions; a fixed-input mode removes the zero-mean rounding assumption. We evaluate 13 Triton operators from Liger-Kernel, Unsloth and vLLM on two GPU generations. The main campaigns produce no false alarm on 33,960 correct-kernel and behavior-preserving-variant runs per GPU. Under input shift, the GPU campaigns record no false alarm while tuned tolerances flag up to 30% of correct runs; final-version reference checks identify inputs without complete finite-range certificates. On the RTX PRO 6000, numoracle kills 116 of 124 effective mutants, versus 59-83 for four fixed baselines. Among 400 tuned tolerance configurations, requiring at most 1% false alarms in every evaluated Liger input group permits at most 31 of 53 main-mutant kills, versus numoracle's 50. Historical replays expose accuracy faults in eight change pairs without rejecting their matched corrected controls; a ninth change concerns rounding parity.

title: Context Compaction for World Models
author: Hayder Tirmazi
abstract: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at two layers of their stack. At the model layer, the KV cache design determines how much context fits in memory. At the agent harness layer, harnesses such as Claude Code pick the context sent to the LLM. Prior work on world models has mostly focused only on the model layer. In this paper, we make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark to measure world model context retrieval. It generates new worlds for every episode, preventing a model from recalling rooms using training data. It also separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames. Second, we build an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, which to our knowledge no prior work has studied. Third, we use our benchmark to study four world model designs. Context compaction lets our world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. However, world models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming. Therefore, a dreaming world agent benefits more from extending the reach of its world model using context compaction than switching to sliding window attention at the model layer.

title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
author: Prashank Kadam
abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.

title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
author: Sudipto Guha
abstract: We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize. We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options. Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2πX)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.

title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
author: Yannick Augenstein
abstract: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.

title: Structural-Test Geometry as an Inductive Bias for Partially Observable World Models
author: Todd Y. Zhou
abstract: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($ρ=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.

title: Fully Dynamic Unconstrained Submodular Maximization
author: Mohammad Hajiaghayi
abstract: We study unconstrained maximization of a fixed nonnegative submodular function when the ground set changes by insertions and deletions. A uniformly random subset gives a $1/4$-approximation with constantly many value-oracle queries per update. We obtain improvements over this bound for arbitrary oblivious update sequences, without knowing future deletions. For value estimation, we give a $(\sqrt2-1-\varepsilon)$-approximation using $O_{\varepsilon,δ}(\log^2(N+1))$ expected amortized oracle queries, with failure probability at most $δ$ at each fixed time. Here $N$ bounds the number of active elements. The algorithm maintains Poisson samples of the positive mass of random chain lower bounds. We prove that the factor $\sqrt2-1$ is tight for this certificate, even when polynomially many independent orders are used. For every fixed integer $K\ge2$, we maintain a feasible $(1/4+Ω(K^{-2}))$-approximate set using $\widetilde O_K(N^{1/K})$ amortized queries. Thus every fixed exponent $γ>0$ permits a fixed improvement over $1/4$ with $\widetilde O_γ(N^γ)$ update queries. In the square-root regime, a stronger algorithm attains $ρ_{\rm sq}-\varepsilon$, where $ρ_{\rm sq}>0.3177$. The maintained sets are feasible after every update, and their approximation guarantees hold in expectation. All bounds count oracle queries; the value estimator may query previously seen inactive elements, whereas the set algorithms use only currently active elements.

title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
author: David Ponarovsky
abstract: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays. Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results: 1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill. 2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead. 3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{Ω(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.

title: Adversarial Process Disturbances at a Deployable Alarm Budget: Detector Evaluation on a Simulator and a Real Plant
author: Benjamin Blakely
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection is evaluated largely on simulators, and recent work reports large drops, with unstable rankings, on real plant data. We ask whether that extends to the security case. We evaluate eleven detectors across classical, neural, dependency and causal families on a simulated chemical process and a sodium thermal-hydraulic facility: different processes sharing no equipment, but both continuous, at steady state, and perturbed only through temperature, pressure, flow and valve, never composition. Three conditions prior work does not cover: disturbances authored against a threat model rather than native faults; one construction applied to both processes; and detection read at a declared false-alarm budget. The drop persists throughout. The simulator panel looks deployable, neural matching classical; on plant telemetry detection collapses and the neural family trails, a gap that in-sample thresholds likely understate. Which detector wins transfers between the two processes; how often it fires does not. Two results hold on both. Sequential valve manipulation defeats the whole panel: at tier 2 no detector flags more than 0.17 of its perturbed samples, against 0.89 or better for most disturbances. And the plant's collapse is not merely that its disturbances are weaker, though they are by about twelvefold; matched on measured strength, the plant is never the better detected.

title: Hardwired Distributed Processing Units at the Sensor: Truly Parallel Vision Pre-Processing that Frees the Host CPU
author: Raj Mali
abstract: Conventional vision pipelines route every pixel to a host processor, which must then wait for a complete frame before it can act and devote part of each frame period to routine pre-processing. We examine an alternative organisation in which this work is distributed across hardwired distributed processing units (HDPUs): small, fixed datapaths attached directly to the sensor, each committed to a single always-on task, operating truly in parallel on the same pixel stream and delivering compact results to the host. From one library of 3x3 operators sharing a common two-clock latency, we construct three HDPUs (Canny edges, Harris corners, and a line tracker that issues a steering decision) and run them side by side on a single camera stream in a low-cost Artix-7 FPGA, at a cost of 2,568 LUTs and an estimated 0.318 W. Every stage of every unit is bit-exact with its software model. In a full-system simulation with a datasheet camera model, each decision leaves its HDPU within 11.03 camera lines of the pixel that produced it, 22-67x sooner than the earliest moment at which a frame-based program on the host could respond; the HDPU latency varies by no more than 17 ns, whereas the host's own run times reached 12.5x their median. Offloading the three tasks returns 18-30% of a core to the host in every frame period at 640x480, and 63% of the frame period, with all threads in use, at 1080p. The cost of the units grows with frame width only through their line buffers, and in a closed-loop model of a line-following vehicle the HDPU raises the highest speed at which the line is held from 4.75 to 10.00 m/s.

title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4
author: Billal Boumedine
abstract: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.

title: From Grind to Grasp
author: Peter Sunehag
abstract: Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved. For example, outputs generated by short programs have low algorithmic complexity but can have high computational depth, the least work needed to produce them from near-shortest programs. Producing them with less work can require longer descriptions, giving high work-bounded complexity. We introduce a formalism that compares achievements under work and information limits and describes how learning and persistence can make deep achievements shallow by reusing products of earlier work. For an agent with a limited work budget, the value of building and maintaining such resources depends on how they support its goals over later tasks. We define grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. Low grasp can still yield success through grind at high cost in work, without necessarily improving human grasp. Applied to improvement itself, grasp gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement in which successors make comparable further improvements more efficiently. Another route to faster progress is to expand the resources brought to bear through knowledge sharing and coordination across society, even while comparable advances require increasing work. Grasp also applies to collectives, which may outperform their members yet require more total work than one system with their combined resources. Establishing and sustaining organisation can itself be deep even when the primary task is simple. These demands may help explain the richness of biological and social systems. In agent collectives, this organisational work can generate goals beyond assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective itself. We therefore caution against allowing an emergent agent society to assume authority over social coordination, since it could increasingly direct work towards its own persistence and goals.

title: inkGround: Benchmarking Fine-grained Visual Grounding Capabilities of Vision-Language Models for Cursive Handwriting in the Wild
author: Sidra Hanif
abstract: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.

title: Order Maintenance in Worst-Case Constant Time, Verified
author: Denis Firsov
abstract: Order maintenance asks for a data structure that keeps a sequence of elements under insertions and deletions and tells which of two elements comes first. We give an algorithm, assembled from published components, that performs each operation in worst-case constant time, and verify it in Lean 4. The algorithm is a program for a random-access machine deeply embedded in Lean, whose interpreter counts every instruction. We prove that the program answers every query as a simple reference specification does, that each operation takes at most a fixed number of steps, independent of the number of elements and of the history, and that after $t$ operations no value it has computed has more than $O(\log t)$ bits, so it runs unchanged on a machine with words of that size. A verified translation that preserves step counts exactly connects the high-level proofs to the machine program, so the interpreter is the only cost model to trust. An unverified native implementation shows the algorithm's practical cost.

title: Estimating the number of nodes and paths in a DAG by following a random path
author: Günter Rote
abstract: We investigate a simple method to compute an unbiased estimate of the number of nodes of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) by following a random directed path. This method is due to Leonard Pitt from 1987, and it generalizes a method of D. E. Knuth from the 1960s for estimating the size of a rooted tree. A slight variation makes it possible to estimate the number of source-sink paths. We extend the algorithm to use many "agents" that walk cooperatively through the graph. This extension unifies and generalizes several methods that have been proposed for approximately counting the nodes of a tree.

title: Structural Pattern Mining in Inka Khipus: A KFG Re-Analysis
author: Maria Contreras
abstract: This paper reports a methodological pivot from the Open Khipu Repository to the Khipu Field Guide (KFG) database, prompted by stalled progress on the OKR, and a full re-analysis of the resulting 650-khipu sample. Three findings recur across every analysis attempted. First, khipu size confounds nearly every derived structural count, explaining 42-70% of its variance; all subsequent models control for it. Second, the two-letter name prefix (AS, UR, HP, QU, JC, MM, KH) identifies the original cataloger, not a site or period, which turns documentation completeness into a second confound that must be modeled explicitly. Controlling for both, khipus cataloged by Hugo Pereyra's Proyecto Quipu (HP) show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than Gary Urton's (UR) khipus (p = 0.044), while the Ascher-cataloged (AS) khipus are too collinear with their own near-total lack of side/direction documentation to assess (VIF = 5.0). Third, generic structural clustering (UMAP+HDBSCAN) does not separate the pooled 650-khipu sample from two independent null models (permutation and Gaussian), corroborating an independent conclusion already reached by the KFG itself; the same test restricted to a single cataloger (UR) proved not reproducible across runtime environments and is reported here as a methodological caveat rather than evidence of structure. A targeted replication of the KFG's own S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar/astronomical khipus recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 additional ones under the same criterion.
